papers.title: A systematic benchmark evaluation of algorithms for 3D tissue alignment and registration with spatial omics
papers.abstract: Recent advances in spatial omics have enabled tissue atlases spanning serial sections, donors, and experimental technologies. Aligning these datasets is essential for comparing spatial organization, reconstructing three-dimensional tissue architecture, and registering sections to a common coordinate framework. However, systematic comparisons of alignment accuracy, computational efficiency, and usability remain limited. Here, we benchmarked 15 tissue alignment and registration algorithms using experimental and simulated spatial transcriptomics datasets across pairwise alignment, three-dimensional reconstruction, cross-resolution alignment, and atlas registration tasks. We assessed spatial-domain and cell-type correspondence, spatial gene-expression similarity, computational scalability, and usability. Simulated datasets with known spatial coordinates additionally enabled direct evaluation of geometric accuracy and reconstruction stability. No single method performed best across all settings: performance depended on the task, spatial resolution, and tissue characteristics, and strong pairwise alignment did not necessarily translate into reliable three-dimensional reconstruction. Evaluation metrics captured complementary aspects of alignment quality, highlighting the importance of using multiple criteria for comprehensive assessment. These findings provide practical guidance for method selection and identify priorities for improving the accuracy, scalability, and accessibility of spatial omics alignment.

papers.title: RFoldSearch enables fast RNA structure search beyond sequence similarity
papers.abstract: The rapid growth of predicted RNA structure databases demands fast and sensitive structural search methods. Sequence-based approaches lose sensitivity for divergent homologues, whereas exhaustive coordinate alignment is computationally expensive. Analogous to Foldseeks 3Di representation, we introduce RFoldSearch and 3Dr, a learned 80-state structural alphabet encoding local RNA tertiary environments. RFoldSearch combines indexed prefiltering, structure-aware token alignment and optional coordinate-based reranking. On held-out RNAsolo 2.0 queries, RFoldSearch retained 81-89% of the family-level sensitivity of exhaustive coordinate aligners and outperformed RiboSeek (RS-20) and BLASTN. On a single CPU core, RFoldSearch searched 531,888 predicted structures in 0.31 s per query, 20-fold faster than RiboSeek with its RS-20 alphabet while using 7.7-fold less peak memory. Searches of predicted-structure databases demonstrated its ability to recover structurally similar RNAs with limited detectable sequence similarity, complementing profile-based sequence search. Recurrent 3Dr words captured conserved local RNA geometries, including fragments corresponding to known RNA 3D motifs. RFoldSearch is available as open-source software, a web server and a REST API.

papers.title: Measuring and reducing segmentation-driven cell-type labeling errors in imaging spatial transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Imaging spatial transcriptomics labels each segmented cell from transcripts that include some of its neighbors RNA. We labeled each cell from its nucleus and its whole mask at equal depth, with two nuclear halves as a null. Whole-cell counts drew small, RNA-poor cells toward their larger neighbors labels. On three platforms, relative to nuclear labels at equal depth, T and NK cells lost 23-53% of their labels in six datasets of five tissues and 4-9% in renal cell carcinoma; this label-only measure matched same-cell protein markers in five donors and, where it differed, understated the loss. In gut, labels alone placed the loss at 58% of T cells among epithelial cells, compared with 24% in the lamina propria. The error lowered immune contact counts mainly by removing T cells; random relabeling, a common robustness test, raised them. Nuclear labels, where nuclei held enough counts, recovered many lost T cells. Imaged nuclei also carried some neighbor RNA and isolated nuclei carried none, indicating that these losses are lower bounds.

papers.title: GinsengMind: An evidence-grounded AI research agent for integrative molecular research in Panax ginseng
papers.abstract: Panax ginseng C. A. Meyer is one of the most extensively studied medicinal plants, with substantial pharmaceutical and economic importance owing to its diverse bioactive constituents, particularly ginsenosides. Despite considerable advances in ginseng molecular research, the fragmentation of genomic, transcriptomic, protein structural, and biochemical information remains a major challenge for investigating gene function and specialized metabolism. Here, we developed GinsengMind (https://ginsengai.nrc.ac.cn), an evidence-grounded AI research agent that integrates species-specific molecular knowledge with large language model (LLM)-guided tool orchestration and structured retrieval-augmented generation. Built upon the telomere-to-telomere reference genome of P. ginseng, GinsengMind integrates 77,266 genes, 154,754 transcripts, and 77,266 protein records. Comprehensive functional annotation using Swiss-Prot, eggNOG, and InterProScan covered 97.00% of the 76,947 quality-controlled proteins. The platform further incorporates 71,046 ESMFold-predicted protein structures, 7,263,004 gene expression records across 94 RNA-seq samples, and 4,813 bibliographic records. Six specialized research tools enable autonomous evidence retrieval and source-linked scientific interpretation through natural-language interaction. To evaluate its performance, we established GinsengBench, comprising 50 curated questions across six research categories. In a blinded evaluation by three experts, GinsengMind achieved a mean weighted composite score of 96.18 across ten core questions, substantially exceeding GLM-5.3 without database access (23.24; mean paired difference, 72.94; 95% confidence interval, 65.19-79.87). Across five shared questions, GinsengMind outperformed nine general-purpose LLMs on average and achieved a score (96.56) close to that of GLM-5.3 supplied with predefined evidence packages (96.88), highlighting the importance of domain-specific knowledge and autonomous evidence retrieval. A case study of the ginsenoside biosynthetic enzyme PgUGT94Q2 further illustrates how integrated molecular evidence can reveal unresolved biological relationships and identify priorities for subsequent experimental investigation. Beyond conventional database querying, GinsengMind provides a foundation for exploring potential biological associations, prioritizing candidate biosynthetic genes, and formulating experimentally testable hypotheses. We anticipate that GinsengMind will facilitate research on medicinal plant specialized metabolism, natural product biosynthesis, enzyme discovery and engineering, and synthetic biology, while offering an adaptable framework for developing domain-specialized AI research agents across other medicinal plants and scientific disciplines.

papers.title: ProteoBridge Connects Proteomics Quantification Outputs to Reusable Analysis Workflows
papers.abstract: Quantification tools for bottom-up label-free proteomics, including DIA-NN, Spectronaut, MaxQuant, and FragPipe, use different table layouts, column headers, modification notations, and parameter files. Downstream applications maintain separate readers for these outputs. ProteoBridge lets an application request the same quantity, such as unnormalized ion intensity, across reports from different quantification tools. JSON parsing rules describe each tools tables, and software-specific parameter parsers read the settings. The rules currently cover 14 tools and are tested on public inputs. A shared parser organizes the reported quantities into one level for each feature type the tool reports (fragments, ions, peptidoforms, peptides, or proteins) and writes the result as AnnData/MuData, Parquet, or DuckDB. A JSON summary records the structure, provenance, and conversion warnings, such as unmapped modifications. Applications can use the apb-catalog API in Python, R, or TypeScript to map the requested quantity to the field that holds it for each tool and version. Researchers can supply a sample table to add the experimental design and a FASTA database to check peptide sequences. ProteoBridge can serve as a common interface for reading quantification results across tools and versions.

papers.title: Structural Landscape of MHC Complexes through Fold Mining
papers.abstract: Major histocompatibility complex (MHC) proteins share a characteristic structural platform formed by two -helices positioned above a {beta}-sheet (1-2 domain), which can accommodate ligands and provide an exposed surface for recognition by protein binding partners. This interaction system is best characterized for classical MHC-I molecules presenting peptides to T-cell receptors (TCRs), one of the most extensively studied mechanisms of immune recognition. However, non-classical MHC and MHC-like proteins reveal that the 1-2 platform is considerably more versatile, supporting a remarkably diverse range of biological functions. Related architectures are also exploited by pathogens, further expanding the diversity of molecular interactions associated with this fold. Yet how this functional diversity relates to structural variation within the shared 1-2 platform and to the diverse modes of recognition employed by natural and engineered binding partners has not been systematically examined across the broader MHC fold. Here, we systematically mapped MHC 1-2-like domains across experimentally determined structures in the Protein Data Bank and predicted structures in the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database using Foldseek, and compiled their natural and engineered binding partners. Our comparative analyses revealed substantial heterogeneity across multiple structural layers, including 1-2 geometry, ligand-binding cavity architecture, and the physicochemical properties and spatial conservation of exposed recognition surfaces, despite the overall conservation of the fold. We further characterized a diverse repertoire of natural and engineered binding partners, revealing distinct structural architectures, interface compositions, and recognition geometries. Together, these findings provide an integrated structural landscape connecting the diversity of the MHC fold with the multiple modes of molecular recognition it supports, offering a comparative framework for understanding these interactions and guiding the engineering of novel MHC-targeting proteins.

papers.title: EpiState-T for representing epigenetic states across time
papers.abstract: Epigenetic information is central to cellular identity, aging and rejuvenation. Unlike the relatively stable genomic sequence shared by most somatic cells, epigenetic states vary across cells and time, making their dynamics difficult to reconstruct from sparse experimental measurements. We introduce EpiState-T, the Temporal Epigenetic State Tensor, to represent selected epigenetic states across intervals and distinguish an observed trajectory from the use of a retained record. In a ten-cell simulation, an explicit reader can act on each cells surviving baseline record. Across 500 paired simulations, mean final distance to the cells own baseline was 0.736 with reading disabled, 0.182 with correctly assigned records and 0.402 with reassigned records. These differences follow from the specified reader. We separately applied the observation and transition tensors to 859,151 CpGs measured in three donor-associated fibroblast cultures before, during and after transient reprogramming. Among sites ending within 0.05 methylation units of baseline, 9.75-15.72% had first departed in treated cultures, compared with 5.37-9.91% in matched mock cultures. The intermediate measurement therefore distinguishes paths that an endpoint comparison merges. These are paths of population measurements: the human data do not track individual cells or establish that cells read a historical record. EpiState-T provides an initial mathematical framework for investigating temporal epigenetic information while keeping state representation, observed change and proposed biological mechanisms distinct.

papers.title: Substrate rigidity suppresses the NRF2 antioxidant program in breast cancer cells
papers.abstract: Matrix stiffness rises as breast tumors progress, but whether rigidity raises or lowers activity of the KEAP1-NRF2 antioxidant pathway is contested: work in breast cancer cells places the antioxidant response on soft matrix, while work in liver cancer places response on stiff. We used publicly available transcriptome data to ask the question across laboratories rather than within one system. Of eleven series identified, four dataset arms passed quality criteria fixed before any biological analysis. Across five contrasts spanning three cell lines and two matrix formats, one program responded in the same direction every time: the NRF2 antioxidant battery was lower on the more rigid substrate in all five. In contrast, SLC7A11, the cystine transporter supporting glutathione synthesis, decreased in all five, by up to 6.5-fold. YAP and TEAD targets did not track rigidity, rising on hydrogels and glass but falling on cell-derived matrix. NFE2L2 and its regulators were unchanged, while targets fell in proportion to their dependence on the antioxidant response element, pointing to control after transcription. An unsupervised partition made without reference to any pathway recovered the same program and survived removal of proliferation genes. In 1,097 TCGA and 1,980 METABRIC breast tumors, the matrix proxy was unrelated to the full battery until immune and hypoxic composition were accounted for, after which the same negative direction appeared in both; and a tumor-intrinsic score excluding macrophage-expressed members showed it more directly. Single-cell and spatial tests produced the predicted direction but could not resolve it, due to limited sample size and because the genes carrying the effect are largely undetectable at spot depth. Reduced antioxidant capacity on rigid substrate predicts greater sensitivity to agents killing through lipid peroxidation, a prediction we set out for experimental test.

papers.title: Cell-type label errors inflate neighborhood effects and can reverse niche claims in spatial transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Niche analyses ask how a cell's neighbors shape its expression beyond its type. The type comes from a label, and labels are imperfect. Here we show that label errors inflate neighborhood effects and can reverse niche claims. A mislabeled cell still expresses its true type, and because cells of a type sit near one another, the neighborhood is credited with what the label misses. Standard practice, which calls labels on the modeled counts and selects cells by them, hid, exaggerated, or reversed this inflation. Labeling one half of each cell's counts and modeling the other revealed it in nearly every population of six datasets. On semi-synthetic colon data, a labeler that over-called one fibroblast subtype reversed claims of the niche method Niche-DE; new draws of the counts and errors spread at random over subtypes almost never did. Our software, nichepeek, reports the direction of this bias in a user's data.

papers.title: gPlace: fast, memory-bounded phylogenetic placement with results identical to pplacer
papers.abstract: Phylogenetic placement methods such as pplacer attach query sequences to a fixed reference tree, thereby establishing their evolutionary relationships to the reference sequences. These relationships can then be used to infer taxonomic classifications or likely metabolic functions. gPlace is a drop-in replacement for pplacer that produces identical results while reducing memory requirements by >3-fold and computation time by >30-fold under typical usage. These improvements are achieved by storing less data per node and streamlining the calculations used to position each query sequence. gPlace can also run within a user-specified memory limit by processing only a portion of the reference tree at a time. Consequently, it can efficiently place sequences on large reference trees that would be impractical for pplacer to process. We demonstrate the importance of these improvements by evaluating gPlace as a replacement for pplacer in GTDB-Tk and CheckM, two tools widely used in genome-resolved metagenomic studies. gPlace is released under the GNU General Public License v3.0 and is available at https://github.com/cmc-aau/gPlace.

papers.title: RIPPLE: learning nucleotide relations in an RNA foundation model
papers.abstract: RNA function depends on interactions between nucleotides that can be widely separated in sequence, yet capturing these relationships remains challenging for RNA language models. Existing approaches primarily learn nucleotide relationships implicitly from individual nucleotide reconstruction or rely on external structural information to model nucleotide interactions. Here we introduce RIPPLE, an RNA foundation model that learns to identify and represent sparse, predictively useful nucleotide relationships directly from sequence. Pretrained on 32.4 million RNA sequences, RIPPLE uses pairwise predictive utility to guide relational learning, transferring training-time supervision into a sequence-only model without requiring structural inputs at inference. RIPPLE improves overall performance across five downstream tasks spanning RNA family classification, ribosome loading prediction, secondary-structure prediction, three-dimensional contact prediction, and splice-site recognition. Mechanistic analyses further show that utility-guided learning improves the recovery of informative interactions and enhances the transferability of learned RNA representations.

papers.title: Alpha-Interferons and CD40: complementary pathways revealed by mGEDO in distinct transcripto-methylomic profiles of patients with Sjögren's disease
papers.abstract: Objectives: Sjogren's disease (SjD) exhibits substantial clinical and molecular heterogeneity, challenging patient stratification and targeted therapies. We aimed to develop multi-omic signatures of interferon-alpha (IFN) and CD40 pathways using mGEDO, and characterize their activity across SjD subgroups and healthy controls. Methods: We developed mGEDO to integrate whole-blood transcriptomic and DNA methylation data from PRECISESADS using BloodGen3 modules, generating continuous two-dimensional patient representations. IFN and CD40 signatures were derived through automated gene selection and quantified using mGEDO Transition Scores. Associations with clinical and biological phenotypes were assessed in PRECISESADS and independently investigated in ASSESS. Results: Among 702 PRECISESADS participants, mGEDO revealed a continuous SjD - control molecular landscape with substantial heterogeneity beyond discrete clustering. IFN and CD40 signatures exhibited distinct, partially overlapping patterns. IFN was predominantly associated with biological disease activity, whereas CD40 provided complementary information, particularly in IFN-negative patients. Combined IFN/CD40 stratification identified biologically progressive subgroups, with double-positive patients exhibiting the greatest immune dysregulation. In 371 ASSESS patients, CD40 and CD40LG expression associations with biological phenotypes were confirmed. Both genes were associated with circulating immune-cell composition. Conclusions: IFN and CD40 signatures reflect complementary, partially uncoupled innate and adaptive immune programs, potentially improving molecular stratification and precision therapeutic targeting in SjD. Whole-blood CD40LG expression may reflect immune-cell redistribution and serve as a potential marker of immune-cell migration.

papers.title: Parent-of-origin classification for diploid genomes using Pooch
papers.abstract: Advances in long-read sequencing have enabled the generation of near-complete human genomes at scale, but trio sequencing has typically been required to determine the parent of origin for each haplotype. Parent-of-origin information is important for studying inheritance patterns and imprinting-associated genetic disorders. Here we demonstrate that parent of origin can be reliably determined for all chromosomes of a Hi-C-phased diploid assembly using differentially methylated CpGs alone. Using 123 near-complete, trio-phased assemblies from the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium, we systematically cataloged differential methylation genome-wide, identifying 880 imprinted differentially methylated regions (iDMRs), including 150 with strong and 730 with moderate differential methylation, including two iDMRs on chrX. From these data we trained an elastic net logistic regression model (Pooch) that predicts parent of origin for each haplotype pair with a mean test accuracy of 0.997 and generalizes across sequencing technologies, cell types, and abnormal karyotypes. Notably, 91.7% of informative CpG features identified by the model were located outside of known iDMRs, suggesting that parent-of-origin differential methylation extends beyond previously established imprinted regions. We further identified parent-of-origin signals on chrX by correcting for the effects of X chromosome inactivation, revealing imprinted differentially methylated regions within an intron of DHRSX and in the promoter of SRPK3, where methylation depended on both parent of origin and X chromosome inactivation status. Our results show that it is now possible to achieve haplotype-resolved diploid genome assemblies routinely and determine maternal and paternal haplotypes for all chromosomes without the need for trios.

papers.title: BYSTER: multimodal graph learning resolves bystander versus tumor-specific T cell states in the tumor immune microenvironment
papers.abstract: Bystander T cells infiltrate tumors without recognizing tumor antigens and constitute a substantial component of the tumor microenvironment. Whether they are passive residents or active participants in antitumor immunity, and how they influence immunotherapy response, remains poorly understood, largely because transcriptional states and T-cell receptor (TCR) sequences alone do not reliably resolve antigen specificity. Here, we developed BYSTER, a heterogeneous graph neural network that integrates transcriptional representations with paired TCR representations through cross-modal message passing at metacell and metaTCR resolution. Across three datasets with distinct definitions of tumor specificity, BYSTER achieved mean AUROCs of 0.729 to 0.920, outperforming unimodal and conventional multimodal baselines, and ablation analyses confirmed the contribution of cross-modal message passing. Application to lung and pancreatic cancer cohorts revealed distinct biological characteristics of the two predicted populations. Bystander T cells were enriched for naive and memory subsets and MAIT-like cells expressing SLC4A10, and exhibited inflammatory and cellular stress-associated programs, including TNF signaling via NF-{kappa}B and hypoxia. Notably, these transcriptional patterns were consistent across lung and pancreatic cancers, with tumor-specific T cells showing enrichment of cell cycle and proliferation-associated programs in both cancer types. Spatial analyses further revealed distinct inferred communication patterns, with bystander T cells showing associations with inflammatory ligand-receptor interactions involving myeloid populations. Responders to immunotherapy contributed a larger proportion of the predicted bystander compartment, suggesting an association between bystander T-cell abundance and an immune-responsive microenvironment. BYSTER thus links predicted T-cell antigen specificity to transcriptional states, spatial organization and clinical response, highlighting the potential importance of bystander T cells in tumor immunity.

papers.title: Auditable AI agents for verifiable end-to-end scientific analysis
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents are evolving from research assistants into end-to-end executors, yet their capacity to generate conclusions at scale outpaces rigorous verification. Here we introduce an auditability-centred paradigm for scientific automation, wherein trust relies not on generative capability or self-evaluation, but on whether claims can be independently traced to primary evidence, reviewed and corrected. Moving beyond post-hoc checks, we embed verification throughout the research lifecycle via four principles: grounded knowledge, bounded execution, evidence-backed results and independent verification. We instantiate this paradigm in EvoTrace for viral evolutionary analysis. Distilling peer-review critiques and methodological literature, we curated 13 principles, 236 pitfalls and 50 analytical units - validating 47 across a six-tier hierarchy - to encode methodological limits as executable constraints. Across simulated benchmarks, six viral datasets and an end-to-end Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) study, claim-evidence auditing compiled evidence packages for all 233 analyses (flagging 26 incomplete evidentiary chains), while independent numerical and figure audits rectified 17 flaws, including three blocker-level errors. For CCHFV, EvoTrace intercepted a data-contradictory claim, recalibrating 'no reassortment candidates' to 'no high-confidence candidates'. By co-delivering verification evidence, auditable automation shifts AI-driven science from autonomous generation to continuous scrutiny and correction.

papers.title: PRS-LDmix: ancestry-mixed linkage disequilibrium reference panels for polygenic risk prediction in diverse and admixed cohorts
papers.abstract: Polygenic risk scores (PRS) are less accurate outside European ancestry, which risks widening health disparities as they move into clinical use. One reason is linkage disequilibrium (LD), the correlation between nearby variants, which differs between ancestries. Bayesian methods such as PRS-CS model LD across all variants jointly, using a reference panel matched to the ancestry of the genome-wide association study (GWAS). Multi-ancestry extensions such as PRS-CSx pair each ancestry with its own panel and require separate summary statistics for each ancestry. However, these are often incomplete or restricted, so scores are frequently built from the combined meta-analysis, whose LD is a mixture that no single panel matches. In practice, the majority-ancestry panel is typically used. Here, we introduce PRS-LDmix, which builds ancestry-specific LD panels from a 32,953-individual, 29-population reference, aligned to shared blocks and SNPs, and averages them in the cohort's ancestry proportions, replacing PRS-CS's LD input without changing its prior or sampler. In simulated GWAS mixing European with African, East Asian or South Asian ancestry, the mixed panel matched the true LD more closely than the majority-ancestry panel. Once the ancestries were balanced, the choice of panel shifted the scores beyond PRS-CS's own run-to-run variation, most for European and African ancestry, and PRS-LDmix was more accurate than the majority-ancestry panel, though not always more accurate than the other ancestry's own panel.

papers.title: Learning the Malignant Transformation of Lung Adenocarcinoma Cells Using Explainable AI
papers.abstract: Tumor evolution in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) drives drug resistance and disease progression, yet the cellular transitions underlying the malignant transformation of cells remain poorly understood. Comparing this progression of cancer cells across patients is challenging owing to substantial inter-patient cell heterogeneity. Here, based on single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) data of 227 patients with LUAD including 422,727 tumor cells, we conducted a comprehensive investigation of tumor cell progression and developed Global Tumor Time (GTT), a continuous measure of tumor cell progression across patients. GTT provided a scalable and biologically meaningful metric of tumor progression that aligned with clinicopathological, transcriptomic and spatial characteristics of malignancy and demonstrated robust prognostic performance (C-index = 0.60), which was further validated in two external datasets comprising snRNA-seq (C-index = 0.66) and bulk RNA sequencing (C-index = 0.61). Using explainable AI to investigate the molecular correlates of GTT, we identified two distinct transcriptional programs associated with early and late progression states. These findings establish a scalable and interpretable framework for reconstructing malignant cell transformation across patients and allow for investigating the biology of tumor progression at single-cell resolution.

papers.title: GeneScribe - a tool for fact extraction and gene summarization using Large Language Models (LLMs)
papers.abstract: The rapid growth of biological data presents major challenges for expert curation and integration of gene information into biological knowledgebases such as the Alliance of Genome Resources (Alliance), limiting data discovery, analysis and dissemination. The current automated approach to gene summary generation at the Alliance relies on curated data and a combination of rule-based and optimization algorithms. While effective, this method is limited by the timely availability of curated annotations, and prone to producing redundant or fragmented descriptions that may obscure the key biological roles of a gene. To address these limitations, we developed GeneScribe, a tool that leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to automate and scale the generation of gene function summaries. GeneScribe employs a two-step workflow: (i) automated fact extraction from the scientific literature, producing gene-specific statements with related provenance without needing manual curation (ii) synthesis of concise, modular and rigorous summaries of gene function from the extracted facts. GeneScribe can provide automated updates to genes with existing summaries and generate timely new summaries directly from the literature for genes that lack one. This will reduce latency in including emerging findings while broadening genomic coverage of the automated gene summaries at the Alliance.

papers.title: scRefine: hierarchical and contrastive learning for biologically faithful single-cell atlas integration and annotation
papers.abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq) studies increasingly encompass diverse tissues, donors, disease contexts, and sequencing platforms, resulting in large-scale datasets characterized by substantial technical heterogeneity and inconsistent cell-type annotations. These datasets offer unprecedented opportunities to resolve fine-grained cellular diversity and identify tissue-specific, developmental, and disease-associated cell states. However, existing integration and annotation approaches often struggle to preserve rare or transcriptionally subtle subpopulations, depend heavily on extensively labelled reference datasets or predefined cell-type taxonomies, and can generate latent representations that obscure biologically meaningful lineage relationships and fine-scale cellular structure. We present scRefine, an annotation-aware contrastive learning framework for integrating heterogeneous single-cell RNA-seq datasets while refining cell identities from partially labelled data. scRefine learns a biologically structured latent space, enabling improved resolution of rare and transcriptionally similar populations. In particular, scRefine better separates rare or biologically distinct populations that exhibit convergent or overlapping translational states than other integration methods. For example, scRefine cleanly separates SPP1+ melanocytic tumor cells from SPP1+ tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), indicating that it preserves lineage-specific biological identity despite shared tumor-associated programs. Beyond cell-state resolution, scRefine also preserves continuous biological structure, as demonstrated by its ability to recapitulate the developmental trajectory of the frontal brain in a manner consistent with the patterns reported in the original study. scRefine also calculates a confidence score by estimating cluster membership using nearest neighbour computations for each cell, which aids in defining cells with ambiguous or mixed transcriptional signatures. Across multi-tissue immune atlases spanning 92 fine-grained classes, scRefine consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in accuracy, rare population recovery, and generalization to unseen datasets. scRefine also maintains high annotation fidelity even when trained with only 1 to 5% labelled cells, greatly reducing the training effort and increasing the generalizability. scRefine is available as an open-source package and offers a robust foundation for constructing coherent, high resolution cell-type reference atlases across studies and technologies.

papers.title: GlycoBind: a general toolkit for protein-glycan binding prediction
papers.abstract: Protein-glycan recognition controls immune responses, host-pathogen adhesion, cell signalling and the functional organization of the glycocalyx. Computational models can predict protein binding to monosaccharides or short oligosaccharides, but predicting binding to structurally diverse intact glycans remains challenging. Here we present GlycoBind, a general toolkit that accepts a protein structure in Protein Data Bank (PDB) format and an International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC)-condensed glycan, and returns a binding score without requiring a protein-glycan complex or a docking pose. GlycoBind adopts the frozen residue-state representation of DeepGlycanSite, a carbohydrate-binding-site predictor, and combines this protein representation with frozen GlycanGT graph representations through a compact trainable classifier. Across five protein-grouped holdouts, GlycoBind achieved a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.767. On six external glycan-array datasets after exact protein and glycan cleaning for both models, GlycoBind showed higher aggregate binding-strength ranking performance and stronger recovery of high-intensity binding pairs than the existing models. By prioritizing high-intensity pairs for experimental follow-up, GlycoBind may support mechanistic studies of protein-glycan recognition and the rational development of glycan-targeted therapeutics.

papers.title: A Single-Cell Transcriptomic Atlas of Human Heart Organoids across Differentiation Protocols
papers.abstract: Human pluripotent stem cell-derived heart organoids have emerged as powerful models of human cardiac development, disease, and therapeutic responses. Here, we present the first integrated single-cell transcriptomic atlas of human cardiac organoids, combining 16 datasets generated across diverse differentiation strategies into a unified reference framework. The atlas resolves protocol-dependent effects on lineage composition, developmental fidelity, and cellular maturation, enabling direct comparison of cardiac organoid systems across the field. Mapping to fetal and adult heart references demonstrates that organoid-derived populations faithfully recapitulate early first-trimester developmental states, with maturation representing the major remaining bottleneck. The analysis identifies reproducible generation of epicardial and coronary vascular lineages, reveals distinct trade-offs between cellular diversity and maturation across protocols, and benchmarks organoids against complementary 3D cardiac models and newly generated datasets. Finally, drug-target analyses expose signaling pathways that remain insufficiently represented in vitro. This community resource provides a standardized framework for evaluating, comparing, and improving human cardiac differentiation models.

papers.title: Deep Learning Prediction of DNA Damage Response Protein Signaling from H&E Histopathology and Reverse-Phase Protein Arrays in Pan-Gynecologic and Breast Cancers
papers.abstract: Defects in homologous recombination and the DNA damage response (DDR) make gynecologic and breast tumors sensitive to platinum chemotherapy and PARP inhibitors, but identifying them requires costly genomic testing that reads permanent genomic scars rather than current pathway activity. Routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) slides are available for nearly every patient. This project asked whether H&E morphology carries information about functional DDR protein signaling across five cancer types in a single model. We matched 1,673 diagnostic whole-slide images from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) to Level 4 reverse-phase protein array (RPPA) data for 1,527 patients with breast (BRCA, n = 858), endometrial (UCEC, n = 403), cervical (CESC, n = 146), ovarian (OV, n = 72), and uterine carcinosarcoma (UCS, n = 48) tumors. Slides were tiled at 0.5 m/px and Macenko-normalized, yielding 20.4 million tiles. Tiles were embedded with two frozen pathology foundation models, UNI2-h and Virchow2. A gated attention-based multiple instance learning (ABMIL) network jointly regressed six RPPA pathway scores, including a DNA_damage composite of 11 DDR proteins. Performance was assessed by out-of-fold Spearman correlation under 5-fold, cancer-type-stratified, site-grouped cross-validation and compared against a baseline that predicts each patient's cancer-type mean. Predicted DNA_damage correlated with measured values ({rho} = 0.43 for both encoders) and exceeded the cancer-type baseline ({rho} = 0.31; {Delta} {rho} = +0.13). The signal held within cancer types (within-type {rho} = 0.29 for UNI2-h, 0.30 for Virchow2). With the original UNI encoder, it survived site-held-out folds with residualized targets (within-type {rho} = 0.26), and it vanished when targets were shuffled within cancer type (within-type {rho} [≤] 0.00 for all three encoders). All six pathway scores were predicted above baseline; Cell_cycle was strongest ({rho} {approx} 0.59). In interpretability analyses, the top 10 attention tiles per slide contained more tumor (+1.8 SD), larger tumor nuclei (+1.0 to +1.3 SD), and fewer lymphocytes (-0.6 SD) than the bottom 10 tiles; 13 of 14 morphometric features differed (q < 0.05). Attention agreed with Integrated Gradients (median {rho} {approx} 0.70). Routine H&E contains a moderate, reproducible signal of DDR protein abundance beyond cancer type, concentrated in tumor-dense regions with enlarged nuclei. Separating this signal from proliferation and predicting phosphorylated CHK1 and CHK2 directly are the next steps toward a functional, slide-based DDR biomarker.

papers.title: PMRIPrep: automated preprocessing and quantification of DSC and DCE MRI
papers.abstract: While dynamic susceptibility contrast (DSC) MRI measures hemodynamics and dynamic contrast-enhanced (DCE) MRI characterizes vascular permeability, quantitative values from both modalities remain processing-dependent. We present PMRIPrep, a Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS) App for automated DSC and DCE preprocessing and quantification. PMRIPrep adapts to available acquisitions and metadata, integrates both modalities within a session, and supports four DSC deconvolution methods and four DCE pharmacokinetic models. In DSC simulations with 4% cerebral blood volume and signal-to-noise ratio 50, pooled median absolute cerebral blood flow error was 13-19% across methods. Median Ktrans bias remained [≤]2% across four model-matched DCE configurations over 0-10% noise. End-to-end OSIPI analyses yielded DCE accuracy and clinical test-retest repeatability scores of 0.85 and 0.85, respectively. Outputs follow BIDS-Derivatives conventions and include machine-readable provenance and visual quality-control reports. PMRIPrep is freely available as a containerized application.

papers.title: Archetypal analysis provides interpretable mixture representations of microbiome community structure
papers.abstract: Microbiome studies routinely reduce high-dimensional community profiles to a small number of coordinates for visualization and comparison. Ordination methods are powerful for detecting compositional differences, but their axes are often difficult to translate into explicit microbial community configurations; conversely, hard clustering can impose discrete states on variation that is frequently continuous. Here we evaluate Archetypal Analysis (AA) as an intermediate representation in which each microbiome is expressed as a convex combination of a small number of data-supported extreme community profiles. Across three applications, AA recovered biologically recognizable structure while preserving graded variation among samples. In a multi-biospecimen human microbiome dataset, different sample-source categories occupied characteristic regions of archetype space, while stool samples were represented by heterogeneous mixtures of archetypal profiles. In an early-life gut microbiome dataset, archetype usage changed systematically with age, describing microbial succession as changing contributions from community endpoints. In domestic dogs spanning forager, agrarian, pastoralist, urban, and industrialized lifestyles, groups showed characteristic but non-discrete combinations of archetypes, supporting generality across host species and ecological contexts. Across the displayed K-sensitivity analyses, the principal sample-source and early-life organization remained recognizable as model resolution changed, while repeated initialization and resampling analyses recovered similar archetypal structure. Held-out samples projected onto fixed training-derived archetypes retained metadata-associated organization within each dataset. Bray-Curtis principal coordinates analysis recovered the same broad biological structure, indicating that the value of AA is interpretive rather than simply greater separation, while taxa prioritized by AA retained substantial predictive information relative to equally sized random taxon sets. Together, these results support AA as a complementary microbiome representation that connects low-dimensional sample coordinates directly to interpretable taxonomic profiles and provides a natural framework for describing ecological states, gradients, and transitions without hard cluster assignments.

papers.title: mRNAspect: Real-Time Quality Control of Therapeutic mRNA with N1-Methylpseudouridine Bias Correction Using Nanopore Direct RNA Sequencing
papers.abstract: Quality attributes of therapeutic mRNA include sequence identity, transcript completeness, and poly(A) tail length. While these attributes require monitoring from development through manufacturing, each needs a separate assay. Nanopore direct RNA sequencing enables rapid quality control because it measures all three on the same molecules within a single run, and the resulting data are available during sequencing. However, N1-methylpseudouridine (m1{Psi}), which often replaces uridine in therapeutic mRNAs, alters the nanopore signal, biasing basecalling and poly(A) estimation. We present mRNAspect, a pipeline combining real-time analysis and m1{Psi} bias correction. mRNAspect includes a fine-tuned basecaller and a poly(A) correction based on the reference sequence. mRNAspect is a packaged macOS app that ingests POD5 or BAM files by watching the MinKNOW output directory as sequencing proceeds. Its graphical user interface shows the latest snapshot of the results, and it writes HTML reports as each input file is processed and a PDF report when the run is finished. When measured on Linux with a single NVIDIA RTX 2080 Ti, each 3-min batch of sequencing (about 5,700 reads) was processed in 38 s. The basecaller was fine-tuned on in vitro transcribed (IVT) constructs and cDNA-IVT libraries. Across 10 m1{Psi} constructs held out from training, the fine-tuned basecaller reduced the error rate from 20.1% to 7.2%, compared with 3.0% for unmodified RNA. A poly(A) correction was fitted to constructs with both modified and unmodified pairs. The correction accounts for the fraction of uridine in the reference sequence and the number of uridines within the 12-nt sequence adjacent to the tail. Across eight constructs, the correction reduced the poly(A) tail length difference between modified and unmodified pairs from up to 9.0 nt to within 1.8 nt.

papers.title: BRIDGE: Backbone Representation for Inverse-folding-Driven Generalizable RNA Encoding
papers.abstract: RNA recognizes small molecules and proteins through their three dimensional structures, but sparse functional annotations limit task specific learning of transferable structural features. We present BRIDGE, an inverse-folding encoder pretrained on 2,501 RNA chain records from experimental structures. Each nucleotide is represented by its phosphorus atom and five ribose atoms (P, C1', C2', C3', C4', O4'). Base coordinates are not encoder inputs. From these atoms, the encoder is trained to predict nucleotide identity, solvent accessible surface area (SASA) and base geometry. With matched readouts, frozen BRIDGE representations reach a three-model ensemble pooled average precision (AP) of 0.627 for external ligand-binding site prediction and 0.647 for RNA-protein interface prediction, compared with 0.503 and 0.516 for frozen, randomly initialized encoders. Under the evaluated full-adaptation recipes, pretrained initialization reaches AP 0.703 for ligand binding and 0.641 for protein interfaces, versus 0.635 and 0.623 for training from scratch. Sequence-only pretraining, without SASA or base-geometry targets, also transfers to both tasks. Whether the base-geometry objectives add further value depends on the task and adaptation mode. In decoy ranking and apo/holo evaluations, transfer depends on the readout and the test set, and small target panels and downstream training overlap in the apo/holo evaluation limit broader conclusions. These results support inverse-folding pretraining as a route to transferable RNA structural representations that do not require observed base coordinates at inference.

papers.title: Genome-guided vs transcriptome-guided mapping: systematic evaluation of RNA-seq quantification bias for tandemly duplicated genes in model and crop plants
papers.abstract: Accurate quantification of RNA-seq data is fundamental to modern plant biology. The choice of mapping strategy and aligner critically determines expression quantification accuracy and shapes the quality of downstream biological analyses. However, a pervasive yet often underappreciated challenge is the accurate quantification of genes located within tandemly duplicated arrays. Here, we selected six representative plant species (Arabidopsis thaliana and five important crops), and compared RNA-seq analysis results generated from two mapping strategies (genome-guided and transcriptome-guided) using three widely used aligners (TopHat2, HISAT2, and STAR). Our results reveal pervasive alignment errors in genome-guided strategies, arising primarily from misaligned reads spanning tandem gene duplicates, a gene class that plays important roles in plant defense and stress responses, detoxification, and secondary metabolism. TopHat2 with the transcriptome-guided strategy yielded the most accurate alignments, whereas transcriptome-guided HISAT2 and STAR corrected most, but not all, of the errors. Transcriptome-guided mapping also demonstrates superior performance over the genome-guided approach on simulated RNA-seq benchmark datasets. Moreover, in functional enrichment analysis, the transcriptome-guided strategy outperformed the genome-guided one in retrieving gene sets biologically relevant to the processes under study. Overall, this study provides a systematic evaluation of how mapping strategies and software selections affect RNA-seq quantification for tandem gene duplicates, and offers a valuable reference for standardizing plant RNA-seq analytical workflows, particularly for studies investigating biology processes regulated by tandem gene duplicates.

papers.title: A noise-corrected metric for evaluating spatial transcriptomics predicted from histology
papers.abstract: Deep learning methods that predict spatial transcriptomics from histology offer scalable molecular profiling of clinical cohorts. However, conventional correlation metrics overstate prediction quality across whole sections by crediting models for recognizing broad tissue regions, and understate fine-scale prediction quality because sampling noise dominates sparse RNA counts. To resolve this, we introduce the reproducible-signal correlation (RSC) metric. RSC randomly splits RNA counts into two halves to separate reproducible signal from sampling noise across spatial scales and within tissue regions or cell classes. Across 12 spot-level and three single-cell methods, RSC revealed that most models capture broad tissue patterns but largely miss differences between neighboring spots or cells, which whole-section correlation overlooks. Within malignant cells, RSC distinguished methods that genuinely capture part of the cell-to-cell heterogeneity from those whose scores across all cells were inflated by cell-type composition. Guided by RSC, we designed a pairwise difference loss between neighboring spots that improved fine-scale predictions on average across 11 models. RSC thus provides a foundation for benchmarking predictions, guiding model design and determining which spatial analyses histology can support.

papers.title: VenusPheno: Transfer-Guided Task Grouping for Multi-Task Bacterial Phenotype Prediction
papers.abstract: Understanding how genomic information gives rise to bacterial phenotypes is a fundamental problem in biology. Genome-level prediction requires models that integrate information from thousands of proteins, while related phenotypes may share genomic signals. However, not all phenotype tasks benefit from being learned together, and suitable task groups can be difficult to define from biological knowledge alone. We present VenusPheno, a framework that combines multiple-instance learning over pretrained ProtT5 protein embeddings with transfer-guided multi-task learning. An attention-based Set Transformer aggregates the proteins in each genome into a genome-level representation. We evaluate VenusPheno on 14 binary phenotype tasks from 12,178 bacterial genomes using genus-disjoint splits. Under single-task training, VenusPheno outperforms computational, conventional machine-learning, and deep-learning baselines in terms of mean balanced accuracy. We then use leave-one-task-out analysis to estimate directed transfer relationship between phenotypes, revealing both beneficial and detrimental interactions. Grouping tasks based on these transfer relationships further improves mean balanced accuracy over independent training and joint training of all tasks. Although inferred without biological priors, the resulting groups are consistent with biologically plausible relationships among phenotypes. VenusPheno therefore combines accurate phenotype prediction with a data-driven strategy for determining which tasks should be learned together. The PyTorch implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/YJinling/VenusPheno.

papers.title: A modular decomposition framework of the CHO transcriptome reveals lineage, genomic, and process-responsive cell states
papers.abstract: Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) transcriptomic studies have generated diverse datasets across parental lineages, cell-line development histories, and culture conditions. However, the transcriptional programs underlying this heterogeneity remain difficult to compare and interpret across studies. Here, we asked whether heterogeneous CHO transcriptomes could be organized into reproducible and biologically interpretable transcriptional modules. To address this, we assembled a discovery compendium of 778 quality-controlled RNA-seq samples spanning multiple parental lineages, engineered cell backgrounds, culture conditions, and perturbations, and applied robust multi-run independent component analysis, resulting in 105 independently modulated gene sets, termed iModulons. To accommodate mammalian regulatory and genomic complexity, we interpreted these modules by integrating gene function, activity-metadata associations, promoter motifs, genomic localization, and RNA-biotype composition. The iModulons captured lineage-associated variation, chromosomal enrichment, and responses to temperature downshift and antiviral stimulation, together with an ATF4-associated amino-acid-stress program. Projection of 377 independent samples onto the discovery-derived iModulons reproduced selected lineage- and process-associated activity patterns and captured a glutamine-deprivation response not represented in the discovery compendium, supporting the transferability of these modules across datasets. When the compendium was expanded to 1,155 samples and ICA was repeated de novo, 89 of the 105 discovery iModulons were preserved among 148 expanded modules, while an additional CHO-DXB11-associated transcriptional pattern emerged. To our knowledge, this study represents the first application of the iModulon framework to a mammalian cell system, establishing a transferable and expandable set of transcriptional coordinates for comparing CHO cell states across heterogeneous datasets and prioritizing programs relevant to cell-line and bioprocess engineering.
